In summary, our research is concerned with
how Mozambique's 2002 curriculum policy for bilingual education, based on learners' languages, has been received and implemented at the local level.
the extent to which the bottom is being empowered to sustain the top down reform of Mozambique's curriculum and language policy, and how the reform is faring as a result.
the extent to which the bottom up can be made to work for the top down, and vice versa, when the two are in conflict.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Mozambique's bilingual education reform is working, but that it has not been implemented in its entirety, and that it will not succeed unless the government and other stakeholders take the initiative and provide the resources necessary to do so.
, in spite of the limitations of the reform, the bottom is doing well in the implementation of the bilingual education modality.
the Mozambican language policy is a good one, and the reform is being implemented, but it is not yet clear whether it will be implemented successfully.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bottom has the potential to sustain implementation, but only if the top and middle are able to provide support and resources.
the bottom can and is, but that the middle can help.
the bottom up is doing well and that the top down is lagging, but that both are needed.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, although the top-down approach to language policy in Mozambique has not been accompanied with sufficient resources, it has been successful in opening up space for the bottom up approach to language policy.
the Mozambican experience suggests that bottom-up implementation is not necessarily a matter of waiting until top-down policies are in place.
, while the top is important for providing legitimacy, the bottom can play a key role in the implementation and sustainability of educational reforms.
